title: The 5 Basic School Plots
author: Nick Nickhart
summary: Storytelling is a core leadership competency, and school leaders can draw on archetypal story structures to make sense of their complex environments and communicate meaning deliberately. The author adapts Christopher Booker's seven basic plots into five school-specific archetypes: the origin story, overcoming the challenge, lost and found, the blind spot, and the pleasant surprise. Each archetype has a suggested narrative structure that leaders can use to surface and amplify stories already unfolding in the school community. Telling origin stories reinforces beliefs and values; overcoming-the-challenge narratives attribute change to specific mindsets and behaviors; the blind spot archetype helps schools make sense of inevitable cycles of growth and decline. The author argues that storytelling is not an innate talent but a learnable competency, and that building cognitive structure around story types enables more intentional sense-giving by school leaders.
points: Storytelling is a core leadership competency that can be learned, and school leaders who deliberately draw on common story structures can practice more intentional sense-giving.

Five school story archetypes — origin story, overcoming the challenge, lost and found, the blind spot, and the pleasant surprise — help leaders recognize and retell the stories already unfolding in their communities.

Origin stories reinforce school beliefs and values with a structure of 'how I arrived and why I stay' for individuals, and 'the idea, the start-up, and why the idea still matters today' for the institution.
The blind spot archetype, drawn from Booker's tragedy, helps schools make sense of inevitable cycles of growth and decline by acknowledging what was working, what was missed, and what is now known.

The pleasant surprise archetype celebrates emergent, unexpected outcomes and is especially powerful for leaders who want to emphasize relational, high-trust approaches over heroic paradigms of leadership.
quotes: Stories drive school culture and it is a reasonable to suggest that story telling is a core leadership competency that can be learned.
From a cultural point of view, telling origin stories can reinforce beliefs and values and a suggested structure for individuals includes: how I arrived and why I stay.
Schools are full of success stories where students or colleagues overcome adversity. I’d suggest a structure of the starting point, the shift and the outcome.

Many school colleagues may experience this during a transition from one headteacher to another because of the inevitable questioning of approaches and the imperative of a new leader to understand and reflect back the organisation.
We can create favourable conditions for improvement but not directly control the outcomes so having a story to acknowledge and encourage condition nurturing can be a powerful leadership move.
Nobody is a born story teller or leader. This competency can be learned and building some cognitive structure can support this development.
If we are better able to recognise the stories unfolding around us, we’re more likely to be able to make sense of the complexity of school life.
